intro:
Joel, the second of The Twelve, sees a massive locust swarm devouring everything—total agricultural catastrophe. He interprets it as God's warning: 'The day of the Lord is near.' The locusts are like an invading army, stripping the land bare. Joel calls for national repentance: 'Return to the Lord with fasting, weeping, mourning.'

Key promise: If Israel repents, God will restore what the locusts ate and pour out His Spirit on all people. Famous prophecy: 'Your sons and daughters will prophesy, old men dream dreams, young see visions... everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved.'

Joel ends with God judging the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat ('The Lord judges') and Judah dwelling secure forever.
outro: Joel's locust plague becomes a metaphor for coming judgment and restoration. The 'day of the Lord' theme—both terrifying and hopeful—runs through the prophets. Peter quotes Joel's Spirit prophecy at Pentecost, showing it's fulfilled in Jesus. The book teaches that natural disasters can be spiritual wake-up calls, and true repentance brings restoration.
